### Problem: XOR Queries of a Subarray {#sec-pref-p5-b}

::: {.p-statement}
An array $a$ ($1 \le n \le 3\cdot10^4$, $1 \le a_i \le 10^9$) and $q$ queries ($1 \le q \le 3\cdot10^4$); each query $[l, r]$ (**0-based, inclusive**) asks for $a_l \oplus a_{l+1} \oplus \dots \oplus a_r$. Return the answers in order.

Source: [LC 1310 · XOR Queries of a Subarray](https://leetcode.com/problems/xor-queries-of-a-subarray/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
XOR is its own inverse: $x \oplus x = 0$. So a prefix XOR table behaves exactly like a prefix sum table, with the subtraction of @eq-pref-range replaced by a second XOR — and it works even though "subtracting" has no meaning for bits.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** Loop the range per query: $O(nq) = 9\cdot10^{8}$ — over the budget of @sec-arr-cost.
2. **Prefix XOR.** $P[0] = 0$, $P[i+1] = P[i] \oplus a[i]$; then $\bigoplus_{k=l}^{r} a_k = P[l] \oplus P[r+1]$, because the shared prefix $P[l]$ appears twice and cancels. $O(n + q)$.
3. Same shape as @eq-pref-range with $(-, +) \to (\oplus, \oplus)$: the pattern generalises to any operation where every element is its own inverse (XOR, addition mod 2, symmetric difference of sets — all three are the same operation on bit vectors).

**Invariant.** $P[i] = \bigoplus_{k<i} a_k$; therefore $P[l]\oplus P[r+1] = \bigoplus_{l\le k\le r} a_k$, all cells before $l$ cancelling out.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Loop the range per query

::: {.form-next}
Answer each $[l, r]$ by XOR-ing the slice directly. Correct and obvious, and $O(nq) = 9\cdot10^{8}$ at the limits — over the budget of @sec-arr-cost, because every query re-reads cells its neighbours already touched.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def xor_queries_brute(a, queries):
    from functools import reduce
    return [reduce(lambda x, y: x ^ y, a[l:r + 1], 0) for l, r in queries]
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> xorQueriesBrute(vector<int>& arr, vector<vector<int>>& queries) {
    vector<int> ans;
    for (auto& qu : queries) {
        int x = 0;
        for (int k = qu[0]; k <= qu[1]; ++k) x ^= arr[k];
        ans.push_back(x);
    }
    return ans;
}
```
:::

#### Prefix XOR: two reads per query

::: {.form-next}
XOR is its own inverse ($x \oplus x = 0$), so a prefix XOR table behaves exactly like a prefix sum table with the subtraction replaced by a second XOR: $\bigoplus_{k=l}^{r} a_k = P[l] \oplus P[r+1]$, the shared prefix cancelling. One build, then $O(1)$ per query — the same range-read shape as @eq-pref-range.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-xor-queries
def xor_queries(a: list[int], queries: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    p = prefix_xor(a)
    return [xor_range(p, l, r + 1) for l, r in queries]     # inclusive -> half-open


for _ in range(400):
    a = [random.randint(0, 2**20) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    queries = []
    for _ in range(8):
        l = random.randint(0, len(a) - 1)
        queries.append([l, random.randint(l, len(a) - 1)])
    assert xor_queries(a, queries) == xor_queries_brute(a, queries)

assert xor_queries([1, 3, 4, 8], [[0, 1], [1, 2], [0, 3], [3, 3]]) == [2, 7, 14, 8]    # the board sample
assert xor_queries([5], [[0, 0]]) == [5]
print("xor_queries OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> xorQueries(vector<int>& arr, vector<vector<int>>& queries) {
    int n = (int)arr.size();
    vector<int> p(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        p[i + 1] = p[i] ^ arr[i];              // prefix xor, identity 0
    vector<int> ans;
    ans.reserve(queries.size());
    for (auto& qu : queries)
        ans.push_back(p[qu[0]] ^ p[qu[1] + 1]); // eq-pref-xor, inclusive ends
    return ans;
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Loop the range per query** is $O(nq)$ time, $O(1)$ extra. **Prefix XOR** is $O(n + q)$: one build pass, then two reads and one XOR per query, at $O(n)$ space for the table. Values up to $10^9$ stay below $2^{30}$, and XOR never sets a bit that no operand had — so plain `int` is enough here, unlike the sum version of the same problem (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $l = r$: a single element, $P[l] \oplus P[l+1] = a_l$.
- $l = 0$: reads $P[0] = 0$, the identity of XOR, and $0 \oplus x = x$ leaves the answer untouched — the padding cell earns its keep again.
- Whole-array query: $P[0]\oplus P[n]$, the total XOR.
- Repeated values cancel: $x\oplus x = 0$, so a range with each value twice answers $0$ — a property the brute force confirms and the table gives for free.
:::
